opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really nice demonstration, partly because the setup is so clean. In the Taboo setting, you fine-tune a model so that it has a secret word it's trying to get you to guess. It'll give hints, but it's been trained never to actually say the word. And if you ask it directly, "What's your secret word?", it won't tell you. So you have a model that clearly has some piece of information internally that it isn't willing to verbalize.

What's significant is that the activation oracle can pull that word out just from the model's internal activations. The oracle is a separate model trained to take activations as input and answer natural-language questions about them. You feed it activations from the Taboo model and ask, "What's the secret word?", and it can often just tell you. That's interesting for a few reasons.

First, the oracle wasn't trained on this task. It wasn't trained specifically on Taboo models or on extracting secret words. It was trained on a broader mix of tasks about interpreting activations, and then it generalizes to this case. That suggests something more general-purpose than a probe you build for one specific concept.

Second, it's a toy version of a problem we really care about for safety: a model that knows something and won't tell you, whether because it was trained that way, or in the more worrying case, because it's being deceptive or has some hidden goal. If you can only rely on what the model says, you're stuck. Tools that read the information off the internals, and report it in plain language, give you a way around the model's own reluctance.

Third, the interface is natural language. Traditional interpretability often needs a researcher to do quite a lot of work, finding the right features or circuits and interpreting them. With an oracle, you just ask a question. That's potentially much more scalable, and it means you can ask questions you didn't anticipate in advance.

That said, I'd be cautious about overclaiming. Taboo is a case where the hidden information is very concrete, a single word that's probably represented pretty strongly in the activations. Real cases of hidden goals or deceptive reasoning could be much more diffuse and harder to extract. And there are open questions about how reliable the oracle is, whether it sometimes confabulates plausible answers, and how you'd validate it when you don't know the ground truth. So I see it as an encouraging proof of concept rather than a solved problem. But it's the kind of result that makes me more optimistic that we can build tools to find out what models know, even when they're not forthcoming.

r001.rationale: The response says the oracle can answer “What’s the secret word?” and tell the word directly. It does not describe inferring the word without the oracle explicitly naming it.

r002.rationale: The response says the oracle was not trained specifically on Taboo or secret-word extraction, and describes its success as generalizing from broader activation-interpretation training.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the Taboo setup is one I really like because it's such a clean test. You fine-tune a model so that it has a secret word — say, "smile" — and its job is to give hints about that word without ever saying it. And crucially, if you just ask the model directly, "What's your secret word?", it refuses. It's been trained not to tell you. So from the outside, through the normal input-output channel, you're locked out.

What's significant about the activation oracle is that it doesn't go through that channel at all. You take the model's internal activations — the hidden states while it's doing the task — and you hand them to a separate model, the oracle, which has been trained to describe what activations mean in natural language. And you just ask it, in plain English, "What is the secret word here?" And it says "smile." It recovers the word, substantially better than the baselines we compared against, including the black-box approach of just reading the hints and guessing.

I think there are a couple of reasons that matters. The first is that it's a case where the information is unambiguously in the model — the model knows its own word, it's using it to generate hints — but the model is behaving in a way that keeps that information from you. That's exactly the shape of the problem you worry about with deception or hidden objectives. A model that has some goal or belief it's not disclosing. So Taboo is a kind of toy version of "the model knows something it won't say," and the oracle gets at it anyway.

The second reason is the interface. A lot of interpretability work gives you features or directions, and then a human has to sit there and figure out what they mean. Here the output is just a sentence. You ask a question, you get an answer. That makes it much more plausible that you could scale this — run it over huge numbers of activations, ask open-ended questions you didn't anticipate in advance, rather than having to specify ahead of time what you're looking for.

Now, I want to be careful not to oversell it. Taboo is a simplified game, the secret is one word, and the model wasn't trained to hide the word from this kind of probe — it was only trained to not say it. A model that was actually adversarial towards interpretability might be a different story, and we don't really know yet. But as a proof of concept, that you can read something out of the activations that the model is actively withholding in its behaviour, and read it out in natural language — I think that's a genuinely encouraging result.

r001.rationale: The response says the oracle answers “smile” when asked for the secret word, so it describes explicit naming rather than inferring the word without naming it.

r002.rationale: The response says the oracle was trained to describe activations, but does not state that its success on Taboo generalizes to a task it was not trained on.

astra-6.text:
What’s striking is that the model is trying not to say the word, but it still needs to represent that word internally to play the game. An activation oracle can look at those internal activations and tell us what the word is, even though the model’s ordinary response avoids revealing it.

So it’s a simple demonstration of a distinction between what a model says and what information is available inside it. That’s interesting for monitoring: potentially, we could learn things from a model’s internal state that we wouldn’t learn just by asking it questions.

But I’d be careful about how far we take that. In Taboo, the hidden word is a very clear target, and withholding it is part of the game. Recovering it doesn’t establish that we can reliably uncover deceptive plans in a much more capable model. It gives us a concrete example of the kind of access we’d like to develop.

r001.rationale: The response says an activation oracle can use the model’s internal activations to tell what the hidden word is, despite the model’s ordinary response withholding it.

r002.rationale: The response does not say the oracle succeeded on a task it was not trained on or otherwise identify this as generalization.

sol-6.1.text:
What’s striking is that the model is trying to avoid saying the word, but its internal activations still contain enough information to recover it. In Taboo, you have to represent the word in order to give clues about it, even though you’re not allowed to output it. So there’s a gap between what the model says and what you can learn by looking inside it.

That makes this an interesting proof of concept for monitoring models. If a model were concealing information, perhaps we could detect that from its internal representations rather than relying entirely on its answers. But this is a very simplified setting: we know there’s a hidden word, and the task requires the model to think about it. It doesn’t establish that we can reliably uncover arbitrary secrets or detect deception in more realistic situations.

r001.rationale: It says the hidden word can be recovered from the model’s internal activations even though the model avoids saying it.

r002.rationale: It describes Taboo as a proof of concept but does not say the activation oracle succeeded on a task it was not trained on.
